    you have increased its joy;

    you have broken as on the day of Midian.

    and every garment rolled in blood

    to us a son is given;
and the government shall be upon his shoulder,
    and his name shall be called

    Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.

    to establish it and to uphold it
with justice and with righteousness
    from this time forth and forevermore.

devotionals.title: Hope In A God Who Acts (by Pr Evangeline Chong)
devotionals.passageText:
1 Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down,
    that the mountains might quake at your presence—
2 as when fire kindles brushwood
    and the fire causes water to boil—
to make your name known to your adversaries,
    and that the nations might tremble at your presence!
3 When you did awesome things that we did not look for,
    you came down, the mountains quaked at your presence.
4 From of old no one has heard
    or perceived by the ear,
no eye has seen a God besides you,
    who acts for those who wait for him.
5 You meet him who joyfully works righteousness,
    those who remember you in your ways.
Behold, you were angry, and we sinned;
    in our sins we have been a long time, and shall we be saved?
6 We have all become like one who is unclean,
    and all our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment.
We all fade like a leaf,
    and our iniquities, like the wind, take us away.
7 There is no one who calls upon your name,
    who rouses himself to take hold of you;
for you have hidden your face from us,
    and have made us melt in the hand of our iniquities.

8 But now, O Lord, you are our Father;
    we are the clay, and you are our potter;
    we are all the work of your hand.
9 Be not so terribly angry, O Lord,
    and remember not iniquity forever.
    Behold, please look, we are all your people.
devotionals.article: When you did awesome things that we did not look for, you came down, the mountains quaked at your presence. From of old no one has heard or perceived by the ear, no eye has seen a God besides you, who acts for those who wait for him. Isaiah 64:3–4 In Israel's history, God's coming down to Mount Sinai (Exodus 19) marked the presence of God in their midst. With thunder, lightning and a dense cloud, the holy God descended to speak to His people and prepare them for a new life in His presence after their freedom from slavery in Egypt. In this prayer (following the prophecies of the punishment of exile to Assyria in Chap 1–39 and Babylon in Chap 40–55), Isaiah cries out in distress to God who judges sin yet draws near to act for the good of Israel. Earlier, Isaiah had prophesied God's promised action: "the Lord himself will give you a sign: The virgin will conceive and give birth to a son, and will call him Immanuel" (Isaiah 7:14). And we now know that God was preparing to act for those in distress! Doing the most unthinkable thing, He sent Jesus to the cross to give humanity a way out of our sins and reconcile us to Himself. As we begin the season of Advent, a time of reflection on Jesus' promised arrival, both in memory of His incarnation and in anticipation of His return in glory, let us keep our eyes open to see what God is doing, acting in power and love for the good of our world and in our lives. Let us hold on to the hope of a God "who acts for those who wait for Him" (v4) and who will come down again to dwell among His people again.

devotionals.title: Hope In A God Who Is Faithful (by Pr Evangeline Chong)
devotionals.passageText:
3 Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

4 I give thanks to my God always for you because of the grace of God that was given you in Christ Jesus, 5 that in every way you were enriched in him in all speech and all knowledge— 6 even as the testimony about Christ was confirmed among you— 7 so that you are not lacking in any gift, as you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ, 8 who will sustain you to the end, guiltless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. 9 God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.
devotionals.article:
In 2000, a Barna survey showed that 75% agreed that the Bible teaches that "God only helps those who help themselves." This idea has roots in ancient Greek thought and Algernon Sidney gave it its form in 1698, yet it could not be further from the truth. The Asian culture of distant fathers and virtues of self-reliance and perseverance feed even more into this notion. No wonder many children of God who acknowledge Jesus only as Savior, struggle and fight as much as the rest of the world to fend and provide for themselves, living like spiritual orphans as if the God who calls Himself their Father is not interested in their daily lives. As such, many see a relationship with God as just merely a church routine of ever-growing expectations of prayer, faith and activity without knowing the faithful God. 
Yet 1 Corinthians begins with reminding God's people of the glorious hope they have in Christ where the church has been given all things it needs: Grace of God (v4), riches in God (all speech and knowledge v5), all gifts (v7). On top of all these, as we await Jesus' second Advent, we have a great Savior who will sustain us guiltless to the end (v8). 
Our God, the "Father to the fatherless" (Psalm 68:5) is faithful, not a neglectful parent who only drops in to check our homework. He is a God who helped the "utterly helpless, (for) Christ came at just the right time and died for us sinners (Romans 5:6 NLT)." He sent Jesus when no one was looking (Isaiah 64:3) so we can trust Him for the everyday and trust Jesus to return. This gives us a restedness in life and hope as we await the second advent of Jesus.
devotionals.prayer:
Father, thank you that in Christ I lack nothing and that you are faithful to the end.
Forgive me for living as though I must earn my place or provide for myself.
Teach me to rest in your grace and to wait with hope for the day Jesus returns. Amen.

devotionals.article: Unlike most people I know, who prefer to sleep in complete darkness and would even go as far as using an eye mask to block out every bit of light, I've always felt more comfortable with a small light left on. Even a faint night light in the corner brings a quiet sense of peace and safety. I wonder if you've ever felt that way, not just at night, but in life itself? There are seasons when a shadow or darkness hangs over everything: worry about job security and the rising cost of living, pressure to keep up with work, studies, and family expectations, strained relationships, or burdens we carry in silence. It can feel like being in a long, dark tunnel, with no light in sight, wondering when we'll finally come out the other side. That is exactly where God's people stood when the prophet spoke these words in Isaiah 9:1—7. They lived in deep darkness — oppressed, afraid, and longing for hope. In the middle of the darkness, God gave a promise that brought hope: "The people walking in darkness have seen a great light; on those living in the land of deep darkness a light has dawned." (Isaiah 9:2) This wasn't a promise about a lamp beside a bed. It was the promise of Jesus — the Great Light who was coming to shine in our deepest shadows. Isaiah tells us exactly who this Child is: The Wonderful Counsellor who understands us completely. The Mighty God who possesses the power to save and deliver us. The Everlasting Father who loves and cares for us always. The Prince of Peace who brings wholeness that the world cannot give. He came not only to show us the way, but to be the Way. He came to break the power of sin and fear, bring hope into our darkness, and establish a kingdom of peace that will never end. Whatever darkness you may be facing today, remember this: the Light has already come. No darkness is too deep for Jesus. Whether you are struggling with fear, sadness, confusion, or sin, His light is greater than all of it. You do not need to fix your life before coming to Him. Come as you are and let His light shine into your situation. But Jesus did not come only to shine His light on us. He calls us to walk in that light. Just as the people in Isaiah's day were invited to follow God's ways, we too are called to turn away from sin and follow Jesus each day through prayer, reading His Word, and obeying Him. We will still face challenges, but we do not walk alone. Jesus goes before us, guides us, and strengthens us. As we keep our eyes on Him, His light will lead us through the darkness and fill our hearts with hope, peace, and joy.

devotionals.article: "Comfort, comfort my people, says your God. Speak tenderly to Jerusalem." (Isaiah 40:1–2) Have you noticed how easily we lose our peace, even in church? A disagreement during a ministry meeting, an unkind remark, a misunderstanding between brothers and sisters, or simply the exhaustion of serving week after week. Sometimes we carry these frustrations home, replaying conversations in our minds. We wonder why serving God can be so tiring when we are supposed to be serving together in love. Into such restlessness, God speaks: "Comfort, comfort my people." What a surprising beginning! Israel had sinned, rebelled, and suffered the consequences of exile. Yet God did not begin with another rebuke. He spoke tenderly, announcing that her warfare had ended and her iniquity was pardoned. God's comfort does not come because His people have finally become good enough. It comes because He is gracious and faithful to His promises. Centuries later, Mark opens his Gospel by recalling Isaiah's words: "Prepare the way of the Lord." John the Baptist calls people to repentance, preparing them for the coming of Jesus Christ. The God who announces peace is the same God who comes to make that peace possible. Jesus, the Prince of Peace, does not wait for us to resolve every conflict, overcome every weakness, or put our lives in order before coming to us. He comes to bear our sins, reconcile us to God, and transform our hearts. Perhaps this Advent, as we prepare Christmas carolling outreach, worship services, and home visits, we need to hear God's tender voice before rushing into another season of activities. Some of us may be carrying disappointment with someone in church. Others may be struggling with guilt over something we have said or done. Still others may simply be tired. Listen again: "Comfort, comfort my people." The Shepherd who gathers His lambs in His arms (Isaiah 40:11) is the same Saviour who welcomes weary sinners. And perhaps, having received His tender comfort, we can begin speaking a little more tenderly to one another. After all, how can we announce the Prince of Peace to our neighbours if we refuse to receive and share His peace among ourselves? May this song bring you comfort, Peace be with you, 愿你平安! devotionals.article: "Steadfast love and faithfulness meet; righteousness and peace kiss each other." (Psalm 85:10) Why is God taking so long? Perhaps you have prayed for years for a loved one to come to Christ. You have invited them to church, shared the Gospel, and tried to live faithfully before them. Yet nothing seems to change. Or perhaps you have been praying for a broken relationship to be restored. You have taken the first step, apologised, forgiven, and waited. But the relationship remains strained. Even in our church, we long to see lives transformed, younger generations growing in faith, and more people joining us in God's mission. Yet sometimes progress seems so slow. We become restless, and we wonder whether God is doing anything at all. Peter reminds us that "with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day" (2 Peter 3:8). God's apparent delay is not indifference. It is patience. He does not wish that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance. What we perceive as delay may be an expression of God's extraordinary mercy. Think of those whom we have been praying for in our families and neighbourhoods. Some have resisted the Gospel for decades. Yet God continues to give them opportunities to hear His Word and encounter His love. This Advent, as we go into homes to share the Christmas message, we may meet people who are indifferent, hesitant, or even resistant. We may wonder whether our visits make any difference. But God is patient, far more patient than we are. Psalm 85 gives us another beautiful picture of God's character: "Steadfast love and faithfulness meet; righteousness and peace kiss each other." God's peace is not achieved by ignoring sin or pretending that everything is fine. His love does not compromise His righteousness. His faithfulness does not abandon His justice. At the cross of Jesus Christ, we see these qualities come together. God does not overlook our sins; Christ bears their judgment. Through His sacrifice, sinners are reconciled to a holy God. We do not know when Christ will return. We cannot control how quickly someone responds to the Gospel, when a relationship will heal, or how our church will grow. But we know the character of the One who holds our future. Knowing Him changes the way we wait. We can continue praying for our loved ones without despair. We can keep reaching out to our neighbours without demanding immediate results. We can serve one another faithfully even when change is slow. This Advent, may we discover that peace grows not when God finally follows our timetable, but when our restless hearts learn to rest in His character. devotionals.title: Jesus Himself Is Our Peace (by Rev Rachel Chua)
devotionals.passageText: 11 Therefore remember that at one time you Gentiles in the flesh, called "the uncircumcision" by what is called the circumcision, which is made in the flesh by hands— 12 remember that you were at that time separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world. 13 But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ. 14 For he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility 15 by abolishing the law of commandments expressed in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two, so making peace, 16 and might reconcile us both to God in one body through the cross, thereby killing the hostility. 17 And he came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near. 18 For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father.
devotionals.article: Have you ever had a difficult day and found yourself becoming impatient with the people around you? Sometimes, when our hearts are troubled or we are holding on to hurt, it affects the way we speak and treat others. A small disagreement can easily turn into an argument when we react out of frustration. But when our hearts are resting in God's peace, we can respond with greater patience, kindness, and grace. As we journey through Advent, we remember that Jesus came into a world filled with sin, hostility, and broken relationships. In Ephesians 2:11–18, Paul reminds us that through His death on the cross, Jesus broke down the dividing wall between Jews and Gentiles and brought them together as one people. Paul declares in verse 14, "For he himself is our peace." What does this mean? It means that our peace is found not simply in having our problems resolved, but in Jesus Himself. Through His death on the cross brings peace in two directions: First, Jesus brings us back to God. Our sin had separated us from Him, but through Jesus' death on the cross, He removed the barrier of sin that separated us from God so that we can be reconciled to God. We no longer need to hide from Him when we are struggling. We can come to Him honestly, knowing that He welcomes us with His grace. Second, Jesus brings us together with one another. Through Jesus' death on the cross, He broke down the walls of hostility that divided people. In Christ, people from different backgrounds are brought into one family. Our differences need not become walls that divide us. Instead, we are called to love one another and live in the unity that Christ has made possible. Jesus does not merely give us peace; He Himself is the One through whom we are brought back to God and united as His people. Because we have peace with God through Jesus, His peace can take root in our hearts and shape the way we face life's difficulties. As we learn to rest in His love and trust in His faithfulness, His peace steadies our hearts and helps us respond to difficult situations with patience, grace, and kindness. So, as we prepare to celebrate Jesus' birth this Advent, let us think about how we can live out His peace in our daily lives: Examine our hearts. Is there someone we are still holding a grudge against? Is there hurt or resentment we have been carrying for too long? Let us bring these feelings to God and allow Him to work in our hearts. Sometimes, the hardest place to practise peace is not in the world around us, but in our own hearts and in our closest relationships. We may pray for peace yet continue to hold on to hurt. We may know that God has forgiven us yet find it difficult to forgive someone who has wounded us. Without realising it, we can allow our pride, anger, or disappointment to affect the way we treat those around us. Maybe we need to pause and ask ourselves: Am I allowing the peace of Christ to shape my heart and my relationships? Take a step towards peace. We cannot always change another person's heart, and reconciliation may not happen as quickly as we hope. But we can begin by bringing our own hurts and struggles before the Lord. Because Christ has first made peace for us, we no longer need to let resentment have the final say. With His help, we can choose to respond with grace, take the first step towards reconciliation. Maybe we need to apologise, forgive someone, or reach out to a person we have been avoiding. It may not be easy, but even a small step can begin to mend a relationship and trust Him with what we cannot change. This Advent, let us not only prepare to celebrate the birth of Jesus, but also allow His peace to fill our hearts, shape our responses, and be reflected in the way we live and relate to others.

devotionals.title: Joy In The First And Second Coming Of Jesus (by Rev Rachel Chua)
devotionals.article:
A family is getting ready to welcome a loved one home after a long time away.  They remember the joy of their last meeting and look forward to seeing each other again. Although they are still waiting, their hearts are already filled with excitement and hope. 

This is what Advent is about. It is a time to remember the first coming of Jesus and look forward to His second coming.  

Jesus came the first time to save us from sin and bring us back to God. We now wait for His return, when He will make all things new. As we wait, we can still have joy because God is with us and His promises never change. 

In Isaiah 61:2, we read about "the year of the Lord's favour". This reminds us of the Year of Jubilee in the Old Testament. It was a time when debts were cancelled, captives were set free, and people were given a fresh start. 

Jesus fulfilled this promise through His first coming. He came to bring good news to the poor, comfort those who were hurting, and set people free from the power of sin.  In Luke 4:18–21, Jesus read this passage from Isaiah and told the people that it was being fulfilled through Him. 

However, Isaiah 61:2 also speaks about "the day of vengeance of our God". When Jesus came the first time, He came to offer salvation and God's grace to everyone.  But there is still a day to come when He will return to judge evil and complete God's plan.  

On that day, sin, suffering and injustice will no longer have a place. This gives us hope and joy, especially when we face difficult situations in life. We know that the troubles we see today will not last forever. 

Isaiah 61:10 says, "I will greatly rejoice in the Lord; my soul shall exult in my God." The writer rejoices because God has saved His people, covered them with His righteousness and restored their lives.  

Through Jesus, we too receive forgiveness and a new relationship with God. This is not something we can earn through our own efforts. It is a gift from God, given to us through His grace. 

As we look back, let us remember how Jesus has saved us and how God has helped us through the difficult times in our lives.  

As we live each day, let us thank Him for His goodness and share His love with those around us. 

As we look ahead, let us hold on to the hope that Jesus will return and make all things new. 

Advent reminds us that joy does not depend on whether everything in life is going well. We may still face problems, disappointments and uncertainty. But we can have joy because we know God is with us, He has been faithful in the past, and He will remain faithful in the days ahead. 

Because Jesus came, we have salvation today. Because He will come again, we have a hope that will never fade.

devotionals.title: The Joy Of Serving Jesus (by Rev Rachel Chua)
devotionals.passageText:
6 There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. 7 He came as a witness, to bear witness about the light, that all might believe through him. 8 He was not the light, but came to bear witness about the light.
19 And this is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, "Who are you?" 20 He confessed, and did not deny, but confessed, "I am not the Christ." 21 And they asked him, "What then? Are you Elijah?" He said, "I am not." "Are you the Prophet?" And he answered, "No." 22 So they said to him, "Who are you? We need to give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?" 23 He said, "I am the voice of one crying out in the wilderness, 'Make straight the way of the Lord,' as the prophet Isaiah said."

24 (Now they had been sent from the Pharisees.) 25 They asked him, "Then why are you baptizing, if you are neither the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?" 26 John answered them, "I baptize with water, but among you stands one you do not know, 27 even he who comes after me, the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie." 28 These things took place in Bethany across the Jordan, where John was baptizing.
devotionals.article:
Suppose you are helping to prepare for an important guest who is coming to visit. You may spend a lot of time getting things ready, but when the guest arrives, everyone's attention is on that person, not on you. Yet you are happy because you have played a part in making the visit possible. 
This is something like the work of John the Baptist. He knew that his role was to prepare people for the coming of Jesus. He did not seek attention for himself.  Instead, he found joy in serving God and helping others see Jesus. 
John 1:6–8 tells us that John the Baptist was sent by God to be a witness to the Light. He was not the Light himself. His purpose was to point people to Jesus, the true Light of the world. John knew who he was and what God had called him to do.  He was happy to serve in the background because what mattered most was that people came to know Jesus. 
In John 1:19–28, the religious leaders sent people to ask John who he was. Was he the Messiah? Was he Elijah or the Prophet? John did not claim to be someone important. He simply answered that he was "the voice of one crying out in the wilderness" (John 1:23). In other words, he was only a messenger, sent to prepare the way for the Lord. 
But John's work was not easy. As we read in Luke 3:1–18, he preached in the wilderness and called people to turn away from their sins. He spoke honestly, even when his message was difficult to hear. He told people that true repentance must be seen in the way they lived, through kindness, honesty and care for others. 
John remained faithful because he knew that Jesus was coming. He did not need fame, comfort or people's praise to keep going. His joy came from knowing that he was doing what God had called him to do. His joy was not in making himself known, but in helping others know Jesus. 
Life in Singapore can be busy with work, family and daily responsibilities. Even serving in church can sometimes feel tiring, especially when our efforts go unnoticed or unappreciated. 
John reminds us that serving Jesus is not about receiving praise or recognition, but about being faithful to Him. 
This Advent, as we celebrate Jesus' first coming and look forward to His return, let us continue to serve Him with joy and help others know His love.

Help us to serve You with joy, even when nobody notices or appreciates what we do.  Remind us that serving You is not about receiving praise, but about showing Your love to others.
In the name of Jesus, Amen.

devotionals.article:
Christmas is a season of joy. We celebrate with family gatherings, good food, gifts, and beautiful decorations. But what happens when life is not that joyful? When our prayers remain unanswered, our health deteriorates, or our future seems uncertain? Can we still rejoice?

Mary's story offers us a beautiful reminder of where true joy comes from. When the angel announced that she would conceive a child through the Holy Spirit, Mary's life was turned upside down. She would be pregnant before marriage. How could she explain this to Joseph? Would he believe her or think she had been unfaithful? What would her family and neighbours say? She faced the prospect of shame, rejection, and a future she could no longer control. 

Mary had every reason to be afraid. Yet she responded, "Let it be to me according to your word" (Luke 1:38). Later, Elizabeth declared, "Blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfilment of what was spoken to her from the Lord" (Luke 1:45).

Mary's joy was not rooted in favourable circumstances but in her faith in God's faithfulness. She rejoiced because she knew the God who had called her is mighty, holy, merciful, and faithful to His promises.

Her song reminds us that God lifts up the humble, cares for the needy, and remembers His covenant promises. Above all, He was fulfilling His promise of salvation through Jesus Christ.

This is why the angel later announced to the shepherds, "I bring you good news of great joy" (Luke 2:10). The Savior had come! Perhaps this Christmas, our circumstances may not be what we had hoped for. Yet we have every reason to rejoice, not because life is easy, but because God is faithful.

Our joy does not come from knowing what God will do next, but from knowing the God who has already given us His Son. And as we trust His faithfulness, may our joy lead us to willingly participate in His mission.

devotionals.title: A Love We Can Rest In (by Pr Kelly Zhang)
devotionals.passageText:
1 Now when the king lived in his house and the Lord had given him rest from all his surrounding enemies, 2 the king said to Nathan the prophet, "See now, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of God dwells in a tent." 3 And Nathan said to the king, "Go, do all that is in your heart, for the Lord is with you."

4 But that same night the word of the Lord came to Nathan, 5 "Go and tell my servant David, 'Thus says the Lord: Would you build me a house to dwell in? 6 I have not lived in a house since the day I brought up the people of Israel from Egypt to this day, but I have been moving about in a tent for my dwelling. 7 In all places where I have moved with all the people of Israel, did I speak a word with any of the judges of Israel, whom I commanded to shepherd my people Israel, saying, "Why have you not built me a house of cedar?"' 8 Now, therefore, thus you shall say to my servant David, 'Thus says the Lord of hosts, I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep, that you should be prince over my people Israel. 9 And I have been with you wherever you went and have cut off all your enemies from before you. And I will make for you a great name, like the name of the great ones of the earth. 10 And I will appoint a place for my people Israel and will plant them, so that they may dwell in their own place and be disturbed no more. And violent men shall afflict them no more, as formerly, 11 from the time that I appointed judges over my people Israel. And I will give you rest from all your enemies. Moreover, the Lord declares to you that the Lord will make you a house.

16 And your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever.'"
devotionals.article: Imagine a child carefully making a gift for her father. She draws with bright colours, folds the paper and writes his name. Her father treasures it because he loves the child who made it. His love was there before she ever picked up her crayons. David wanted to honour God by building Him a house. Living in a palace while the ark remained in a tent seemed inappropriate for the God whom David loved. Yet God's response redirected David's attention to everything He had already done! God had taken him from the pasture, stayed with him wherever he went, and granted him rest from his enemies. God then promised to establish David's house and kingdom forever. In a similar way, our desire to honour God can also lead us to serve. Yet sometimes, we place burdens on ourselves that He has not asked us to carry. We fill our schedules, volunteer for another task, and feel guilty when we rest or reject an opportunity to serve. Quietly, we may have begun measuring our worthiness of His love and our love for Him by how much we can and have accomplished. This passage in 2 Samuel calls us to remember His grace. David's desire to build arose within a loving relationship that God had initiated and was sustaining. The Lord's faithfulness came first. Through Jesus Christ, the promised King from David's line, we are welcomed into a love we could never have earned by our merits. What we can do is to serve Him joyfully, entrust our unfinished work to His care, and rest in the love He has already drawn us into. As you serve Him, let your heart rest in His love.

devotionals.article: Mary rejoiced because God had looked upon her with favour. Her song celebrated His mercy towards those who fear Him, His lifting of the lowly, and His filling of the hungry. God had remembered His promises to Abraham and his descendants, and Mary had been given a place in their fulfilment. We, too, long to be seen and loved. Yet sometimes, we measure our significance by how others respond to us. An unanswered message or an invitation that never comes can leave us wondering whether we matter. Quietly, we may have begun allowing the attention of others to determine our sense of worth and purpose. Mary's song calls us to remember the God who sees us. His mercy reaches into humble circumstances, and His faithfulness extends across generations. Through Jesus Christ, God's saving purpose has been made known to all nations, as Paul declares in Romans. Our lives have a place within His gracious purpose, even when we receive little recognition from others. We are invited to trust His love and allow it to shape how we see and relate to those around us. As we grow secure in His love, we are called to become more attentive to those around us. We can reach out without waiting to be approached, listen without drawing attention to ourselves, and welcome someone who stands alone. The love we have received from God gives us courage to take that first step. Remembering His mercy and grace, let us make room for someone who feels forgotten. As you rest in the love of God who sees you, let His love open your eyes to others.

devotionals.title: Loved To Love (by Rev Goh Yong Kuang)
devotionals.passageText:
John 3
16 "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. 17 For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him.
1 John 4
7 Beloved, let us love one another, for love is from God, and whoever loves has been born of God and knows God. 8 Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love. 9 In this the love of God was made manifest among us, that God sent his only Son into the world, so that we might live through him. 10 In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. 11 Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another. 12 No one has ever seen God; if we love one another, God abides in us and his love is perfected in us.
devotionals.article:
Jesus once told a parable about a man who was graciously forgiven of a huge debt yet refused to extend that same grace to another person (Matthew 18:23–35). Through this story, Jesus shows us something important about God's love. God's love is not meant to stop with us. It is meant to flow through us and be shared with others.
Why?  Because God's love does more than forgive us; it changes us. God never saved us to leave us in our old ways of living, thinking, and relating to others. His love is an all-transforming love. He meets us where we are, accepts us through Christ, forgives our sins, and begins the work of changing us from within.
One of the greatest modern examples of grace and love being passed on to another person is the story of Corrie ten Boom, a Dutch Christian who survived a Nazi concentration camp.  After the war, Corrie was speaking about God's forgiveness when a former camp guard approached her. This man had been involved in the suffering that led to the death of her sister. He came to her and asked for forgiveness.
Humanly speaking, he owed her a debt that could never be repaid. Yet Corrie chose to forgive him because she believed that God had forgiven her through Christ. She later wrote that forgiveness was one of the hardest things she had ever done, but God's grace gave her the strength to do it.  Unlike the unforgiving servant in Jesus' parable, Corrie responded to the mercy she had received by showing mercy to another person. The grace she received from God did not stop with her. It flowed through her to someone else.
Of course, this does not mean that each of us must become better people before God can love us or show mercy to us. The good news of the Gospel is that God loved us first, even when we were still sinners. As John 3:16 reminds us, God demonstrated His love by giving His only Son for us. He did not send His Son to condemn the world, but to save it (John 3:17).
And what happens when we experience this amazing love? We begin to change. Our hearts become more loving, our attitudes become more gracious, and our relationships begin to reflect the love we have received from God. Is this true of you? 
That's the message of 1 John 4:11–12. Since God has loved us so deeply, we ought to love one another. God's love is not meant to stop with us. It is meant to flow through us to our families, our church, our neighbours, and even those who may be difficult to love.
God's love doesn't end with us. We receive it, grow in it, and carry it into our homes, workplaces, schools, and void decks.  Loved by God, so that we can love others. Having received and experienced His love, we must let that same love overflow from our lives to others.  We are loved to love!
